Senses.Note: Guishan says this after Yangshan praises his summer routine and then sticks out his tongue. Fushi criticizes the teacher and disciple together; Guxue asks why the tongue gesture drew the rebuke; Hongzhi turns it into a question for the audience; Zhe’an objects to measuring the two men’s summer practice. In a separate interview Yushan uses the same words after a monk shouts when asked to show his “wisdom sword.” The line faults a self-defeating move in an encounter, not bodily harm.

AlternateTargets: The call is for a flying dragon steed, yet a limping turtle presents itself
SearchAliases: Decree calls dragon horse turtle emerges
Senses.Note: The horse and tortoise contrast is a current teacher's testing appraisal in seven encounters. A bow, shout, or elegant phrase is not necessarily accepted as matching the challenge. The imperial summons is the image used, not a historical event asserted by these records.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Tian'an describes buckets lowered to catch great creatures, a sword at the gate, and a net around the walls. Advancing, retreating, or remaining still each falls into a different trap. He asks for someone beyond the usual pattern to meet him. As soon as one monk steps out, Tian'an shouts and gives the headword, then leaves the seat. The desired steed and appearing tortoise assess this immediate response to his challenge. The source does not record an answer from the monk beyond coming forward; the next evening address about one dust mote and one leaf is separate.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB193.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan. At Yinyuan's formal opening, after incense and the announcement that the assembly should observe the first meaning, Yinyuan says even the Buddhas have no place to set an eye there. He asks how the assembly will observe it and challenges someone to leap out. A monk bows; Yinyuan gives the headword. The subsequent question about what endures ancient and present is another marked question and receives a different response. The line is Yinyuan's judgment of the first monk's bow in this setting, not a monk claiming to be the flying steed or an account of an actual decree.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB196.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanhu Yong. During Yuanhu's birthday address, one monk asks for a saying outside ancient and present and is answered with today's date. Another monk then comes forward. Yuanhu strikes him at once and gives the headword; the monk shouts, and Yuanhu strikes again. Yuanhu's ensuing address compares Shakyamuni's birth with his own coming into the world, testing both sameness and difference before ending with stream and cloud imagery. The headword belongs to Yuanhu between two actual blows; the monk's shout is a subsequent turn, not the headword's speaker or proof that the earlier appraisal has been reversed.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB211.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ji Zongche. At Jizong's opening address, he has likened his arrival to casting a golden hook to gather fierce dragons and asks for a fish that defies capture. A monk asks about upturned nostrils and feet on the ground, then offers the peaceful images of water entering the sea and clouds reaching Cangwu. Jizong answers with the headword. Further monks' questions and Jizong's address continue afterward, including further criticism of attractive descriptions of clarity. The horse-and-tortoise contrast is his appraisal of the offered couplet, not an endorsement that poetic calm has met the original fishing challenge.

At the birthday instruction requested by the layman Yao Xingle, Yingning has pointed to his staff as the means of refining ordinary and holy and urged recognition before birth. A monk asks what person he allows to enter realization. Yingning gives the headword. The monk then invokes the holy figures and asks about their laughter; Yingning says they laugh at his pulling and dragging. When the monk asks about guidance, Yingning says even that is too little, and a further scenic couplet is met with the requirement to know a stream flowing backward. The headword is Yingning's testing answer, followed by continued pressure rather than a simple admission of the questioner.

Senses.Explanation: To revive after being cut off: the records use a death-and-revival image in a recurrent teaching-seat formula and in explicit criticism of that formula. Its dominant fixed formula is ‘let go at the cliff and personally assent and undertake it; revive after being cut off, and you cannot deceive anyone’ (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再甦，欺君不得). Records also place it after ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), beside ‘shed skin and exchange bones’ (去皮換骨), and compare it with a cold ember flaming and a withered tree flourishing again. Tianqi Benrui explicitly departs from the inherited formula: ‘the former sages all wanted to revive after being cut off; I am not like that.’ The entry reports this recurrent sequence and its criticism without deciding what state the phrase denotes.

Senses.Explanation: The repeated opposition licenses a narrow functional inference: the pierced-ear guest is the rare receptive listener, while the common boat-marker remains fixed on the place where something was lost. Fengxue Yanzhao states the pair; Ciji Ziwen Yue, Binya Jian, Guxue Zhenzhe, and Yongji Rong reuse it as a direct answer. The boat-marker half explicitly invokes the person who marks a boat where something was lost and then searches from that fixed mark. The receptive-hearing value of the pierced-ear half is an inference from its repeated opposition to that figure, not a self-gloss supplied by the records.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Nowhere is there a trace; one's bearing lies beyond sound and form
SearchAliases: nowhere is there a trace; one's bearing lies beyond sound and form
Senses.Note: After hearing a tile strike bamboo, Xiangyan writes that there is no trace anywhere and that his bearing lies beyond sound and form. Fushi quotes the verse but asks what the highest move is, ending with a shout. Yezhu raises a whisk before voicing the couplet; Gulin uses a copper censer to test the poem's claim. Lingyin contrasts Xiangyan's response with learned debate, while Yuejiang says the first verse still needed further testing. Sound and form remain present as the teachers question what can be grasped from them.

Senses.Explanation: Everywhere there are green willows to tie up a horse; every household has a road to Chang'an. Present access to the center as available in ordinary places. Poshan Haiming, Yinyuan Longqi, and Dabo Qian use the complete saying in separate recorded teaching works. Fushi Tongxian and Yingshan Zhiyin provide further current deployments. The capital is an image of arrival; speakers still ask listeners to locate the road themselves.

Senses.Note: Liu Yanxiu, a Song layman, is explicitly named as the poet of the full four-line verse in Baichi source. Senses.Explanation: Appraisal-commentary is the public written handling of old cases or verses, and the same word labels the resulting commentarial work or collection. Chan books make it a named layer of case literature: the named commentator addresses earlier verses, and the resulting appraisal-commentary can become a titled collection. Title constructions name Yuanwu Keqin appraising Xuedou Chongxian's verses, Wansong Xingxiu appraising Hongzhi Zhengjue's verses, and Linquan Conglun appraising verses associated with Touzi Yiqing and Danxia Zichun. Daguan Zhenke's signed preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wushan Jingduan gives the documentary sequence: 'from recorded encounters, verses on old cases were made; from verses on old cases, appraisal-commentary collections were made' (由機緣而頌古作，由頌古而評唱集). A poem heading by Guxue Zhenzhe speaks of 'burning Wansong's appraisal-commentary on public cases' (焚萬松評唱公案). Its verbal, nominal, and title constructions are grammatical uses of the same activity and product, not separate dictionary senses. An appended dialogue asks why widespread raising and appraisal-commentary, used to examine old material, is called mastery of the lineage. This hostile question is a stance toward the same public commentarial work, not a second referent.
